summary:
Khabarovsk Krai stands under the national framework of Russia, which in 2023 prohibited legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care outright and under which the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation now supplies the charge on which courts convict. The federal "propaganda" statute criminalises public expression including anything justifying gender transition. Foreigners found guilty under these provisions may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and deported, and the US State Department travel advisory for Russia advises against all travel regardless of personal characteristics while stating that displaying certain symbols, among them the rainbow flag, is a crime.

Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. The "gay propaganda" law carries fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, and at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024.

Enforcement reaches into ordinary employment in the krai. In September 2024 a biology and chemistry teacher from Khabarovsk was forced to resign after video of him dancing in high heels surfaced amid public controversy; in October he filed a lawsuit against the Khabarovsk education department seeking reinstatement, and the case was pending at the time of the June 2025 UK Home Office country policy note.

National enforcement figures set the baseline a visitor in Khabarovsk Krai should expect. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the designated "International LGBT Movement" or displaying its symbols since the November 2023 ruling, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison. HRW also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media, and 257 "gay propaganda" penalties imposed in 2023-24 against 22 in 2021-22.
tangentialFactors:
The trajectory of enforcement is measurable: "gay propaganda" penalties rose from 22 in 2021-22 to 257 in 2023-24, and the post-designation extremism caseload has produced sentences of up to 12 years. Display of symbols is the most common administrative charge, pursued mostly through social media posts rather than street activity, so online expression carries direct legal exposure.

The Khabarovsk teacher case sits adjacent to criminal liability: it is employment and reputational coercion rather than a charge under the propaganda statute, and it shows that conduct unrelated to sexual orientation as such can still cost a resident their post in the krai. The UK Home Office country policy note of June 2025 (page updated 12 August 2026) treats LGBT+ people in Russia as a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

The US State Department advisory is a Level 4, Do Not Travel warning that applies to all travellers and separately flags penalties aimed at LGBT visitors, including arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation.
localsOnly:
Residents of Khabarovsk Krai have no route to legal gender recognition or gender-affirming care, both prohibited nationally since 2023, and no route to same-sex marriage. Consensual same-sex activity is not itself criminalised.

Administrative liability under article 20.3 applies to displaying banned symbols, most often charged on the basis of social media content, and criminal extremism charges carry prison terms of up to 12 years. The Khabarovsk teacher who was forced to sign a resignation in September 2024 pursued reinstatement through the courts against the krai education department, indicating that administrative and labour remedies remain available to residents even where the underlying conduct is treated as public scandal.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Khabarovsk Krai regional statute specific to LGBT expression is sourced in the inventory; the legal basis described here is the national framework as applied in the krai. Whether the krai has its own additional restrictions is unresolved and not sourced.

The outcome of the Khabarovsk teacher's reinstatement lawsuit was pending at the time of the June 2025 UK Home Office note, and no later resolution is sourced. The 139-person anti-LGBT+ enforcement figure for 2022-2024 is a national total with no breakdown by region, so its Khabarovsk Krai component is unresolved.

No krai-level hate-crime statistics, police-incident records or clinic-access data are sourced in this inventory; violence and care-access findings rest on national documentation only.
